items.title: Your first match
items.text:
This walkthrough takes you through one practice round, from opening the app to closing it again. Follow it in order — there are no choices to make along the way. It takes about ten minutes.

Before you start: Concordance needs to be installed. If it is not, see Which download do I need?.

items.title: 1. Open the app
items.text: The first screen is the home screen. It has one large button, START A NEW ROUND, and a Resume round list underneath it. The list is empty until you have a round you have not finished.

items.title: 2. Pick the rules
items.text: Tap START A NEW ROUND. The setup screen opens. Two tabs sit at the top: Teen Bible Quiz and Junior Bible Quiz. Pick either one to practice with. A card under the tabs updates to show that ruleset — how many questions there are, what they are worth, and the numbers for quizzing out, striking out, and fouling out.

items.title: 3. Name the teams and quizzers
items.text:
Each team starts with the name of its side of the quiz box: Red and Green. You can leave those names as they are, or type your own. If you clear a field by mistake, the app falls back to the default for you.

Under each team name is a row for its quizzers. Seated is how many quizzers sit at the table; Bench is how many extras are waiting to rotate in. Use + and − to change them. Every quizzer gets a name field, already filled with a sensible default like Red 1 or Green 2 — type over them or leave them alone.

items.title: 4. Choose how the scores look
items.text: Below the teams are two cards, Modern and Classic. Both keep score in exactly the same way; they only look different. Modern splits the screen into a red half and a green half, with a large card for each quizzer. Classic looks like the paper scoresheet, with one row per quizzer and one column per question. Pick one to try — you can change it later. If you want to know more before choosing, read Modern vs Classic.

items.title: 5. Start the round
items.text: Tap START ROUND. The live scoring screen appears. From this moment on, everything you do is saved the moment you do it.

items.title: 6. Score a few questions
items.text:
Before a question can be scored, Concordance needs to know what it is worth. Tap the value row for the current question, or the SET VALUE button at the top of the screen, and choose 10, 20, or 30.

Then tap the quizzer who answered, and tap CORRECT or INCORRECT. The team's total and that quizzer's own score change straight away. A correct answer moves you on to the next question by itself.

items.title: 7. Make a mistake on purpose
items.text: Tap INCORRECT for a quizzer you meant to mark correct. Then tap UNDO. Everything goes back the way it was — the score, the quizzer's counts, and the position on the screen. This is the most useful button in the app, so get comfortable with it now. See Undo & corrections.

items.title: 8. Record a foul and a time-out
items.text:
Tap FOUL, then choose the quizzer who fouled. A foul takes points off that quizzer; a team foul, which does not need a quizzer selected, takes points off the team total.

To take a time-out, use the red or green time-out button beside each team's name. That team's count goes up. In a real match you would also record interruptions and contests — those have their own button and menu.

items.title: 9. Finish the round
items.text: When the last question is done, tap Summary in the bottom bar. The summary shows the final score, each quizzer's totals, and the announcements the ruleset asks for. From here you can save the round as a PDF or a spreadsheet file, and share it if you like. Tap Done to return to the home screen. See Match summary.

items.title: 10. Prove that it saves
items.text: Close the app completely — do not just press Home. Now open it again. Your round is waiting under Resume round. Open it and you are exactly where you left off, on the same screen with the same score. That is the autosave at work, and it means a dead battery or a crash mid-match will not cost you the round. See Autosave & recovery.

items.title: Tour of the screens
items.text:
Concordance has four screens. The rest of this guide refers back to them by name, so it is worth a minute to learn what each one is for.

Screen What it is for Main areas Home Start a new round, reopen one you have not finished, change the theme or haptics START A NEW ROUND, the Resume round list, the buttons along the top Setup Choose the rules, the teams, the quizzers, and how the scores look The ruleset tabs, the team and quizzer fields, the Modern/Classic cards Live scoring Where you keep score during the round The team scoreboards, the question navigator, the bottom console Summary The final result, the announcements, and the export Team totals, per-quizzer totals, the export buttons

The Home screen also has three small buttons in its top corner: a switch for light and dark, a switch for the tap vibration, and an About button that shows the app's version. See Settings.

items.title: How the screens connect
items.text:
A round always moves forward in one direction:

Home → Setup → Live scoring → Summary

You can go back at any point, and going back is always safe: every ruling you have made is already saved by the time the screen changes. The Done button on the summary returns you to the home screen.

items.title: The two live scoring screens
items.text:
The live screen comes in two versions, Modern and Classic. They are two ways of looking at the same round, not two different apps, so switching between them never changes a score or a ruling.

  • Modern splits the screen into two halves — red on the left, green on the right — with a large card for each seated quizzer.
  • Classic shows a grid like the paper scoresheet: one row per quizzer, one column per question.

There is more on both in Modern vs Classic.

items.title: The bottom console
items.text:
The console is the strip of large buttons along the bottom of the live screen, and it is the only place where scoring happens. CORRECT, INCORRECT, FOUL, Undo, and Interruption all live here, along with the More menu and the Summary button.

One thing is worth repeating: on the Classic screen, tapping a cell in the grid moves you to that question, but it does not score it. Scoring always happens in the console.

items.title: The question navigator
items.text: The navigator is the row of question numbers on the live screen. It shows at a glance what happened on each question, using the same marks the paper scoresheet uses — a circle for an interrupted question, a slash for a contested one, and an F for a foul. Tap a number to look at that question. See Question navigator.

items.title: Alerts
items.text: Goal: know what each on-screen notice means, and whether you have to do anything about it.

items.title: How alerts appear
items.text:
Alerts are the notices that appear just above the scoring console. They are plain text and they do not move — there is no flicker and no sound. Tap a notice to dismiss it; dismissing it only hides the notice, and it never changes the round.

Because the app does not make any sound, the notices are the only way it tells you something has happened. If you have a screen reader turned on, it reads the notice aloud like any other text.

items.title: Quiz out
items.text: Appears when a quizzer reaches the ruleset's number of correct answers — five in Teen Bible Quiz, six in Junior Bible Quiz. It includes the bonus that comes with quizzing out. You do not add anything yourself; the app works it out from the answers you have already recorded.

items.title: Strike out
items.text: Appears on a quizzer's third incorrect answer.

items.title: Foul out
items.text: Appears on a quizzer's third foul.

items.title: Time-out limit
items.text: Appears when a team asks for a time-out past its limit — the fourth in regulation. The request is not counted, and the notice reminds you that a team foul is owed, which you record yourself.

items.title: Contest or appeal limit
items.text: Appears when a team reaches its allowance — the third unsuccessful contest in Teen Bible Quiz, or its final appeal in Junior Bible Quiz. After that, further challenges from that team are refused.

items.title: A tied match
items.text: Appears when the last regulation question leaves the match level. An overtime question is added, and you carry on scoring.

items.title: A value notice
items.text: Appears when a point value breaks a rule of the ruleset — a thirty-point question at one end of a Junior Bible Quiz match, or two thirty-point questions in a row, for example. It is a heads-up only. Nothing is blocked, and the notice returns if you undo the value and enter it again.

items.title: What an alert never does
items.text: A notice does not change a score by itself. Every point — including the quiz-out bonus — comes either from a scoring action you make or from the rulings already recorded. The notice is there to tell you what happened, not to do it for you.

items.title: Dismissing a notice
items.text: Tap a notice to make it go away. Dismissing it does not undo anything and does not change the round, and the same notice can appear again later if the same situation comes up again.

items.title: Autosave & recovery
items.text: The short answer: if the tablet dies mid-match, the round is not lost. Everything you have already recorded was written down as you went.

items.title: Autosave
items.text: Every ruling is saved the instant you make it. There is no Save button and nothing to remember. You can close the app, the tablet can run out of battery, or it can be restarted — whatever was on the screen before the interruption is still there afterwards.

items.title: Resuming a round
items.text: Saved rounds appear on the home screen under Resume round. Tapping one opens it exactly where you left off: the same score, the same question, and the same undo history, so you can still step back through everything you recorded.

items.title: What survives what
items.text:
What happens What you keep The app crashes or is forced closed The round is safe The tablet runs out of battery The round is safe The tablet is restarted The round is safe The app is updated The round is safe The app is uninstalled The round is deleted — save a copy first

If a round needs to outlive the app, save it as a PDF or a spreadsheet file first. See Match summary.

items.title: Deleting a round
items.text: You can delete a round from the Resume round list. The app asks you to confirm first, because deleting cannot be undone.

items.title: If something looks wrong
items.text: If a round will not open, or seems to be missing taps, do not uninstall the app — that would remove the very thing you are trying to save. See Recovering a round.

items.title: How it works
items.text: Rounds live in a small database file on the device itself — see Data & storage. The app never sends anything to a server, so bringing a round back never depends on anything except the tablet in your hands.

items.title: Fouls, contests, interruptions & time-outs
items.text: Goal: record everything that happens besides a correct or incorrect answer.

items.title: Interruptions
items.text:
An interruption is when a quizzer buzzes in before the question has finished being read. Record it with the Interruption button in the bottom console, which marks the current question. On the question navigator, an interrupted question gets a circle around its number — the same encircled mark the paper scoresheet uses.

An interruption also changes what happens next: if an interrupted question is answered wrong, it is read again to the other team and you stay on it rather than moving on.

items.title: Fouls
items.text:
A foul takes five points off. There are two kinds:

  • A personal foul is charged to one quizzer. Tap FOUL, then choose the quizzer. Their score shows an F beside it.
  • A team foul is charged to the whole team — a coach's foul, for instance. Tap FOUL and choose the team option; no quizzer needs to be selected.

A third personal foul fouls that quizzer out. Fouls survive a void: if a question is thrown out later, the fouls charged on it stay in place.

items.title: Contests and Coach's Appeals
items.text:
A contest (Teen Bible Quiz) or a Coach's Appeal (Junior Bible Quiz) is a challenge to a ruling. Both are handled the same way in the app. Each team has a button beside its name in the header — tap it and record whether the challenge succeeded or failed, and that team's tally goes up.

The ruleset sets a limit, and the app tells you when a team reaches it: the third unsuccessful contest in Teen Bible Quiz, or the second appeal in Junior Bible Quiz. Once a team has used its allowance, further challenges from that team are refused. See Alerts.

items.title: Time-outs
items.text:
Each team's time-outs are counted separately. Use the red or green time-out button beside that team's name; the count goes up by one. When a team reaches the limit — three in the regulation part of a match — the app notifies you.

A request past the limit is refused rather than counted. The app then tells you to assess the resulting team foul yourself, because the scorekeeper makes that call, not the app.

Overtime works differently in each ruleset. In Teen Bible Quiz, no time-outs may be taken. In Junior Bible Quiz, any time-outs a team has left carry over, plus one extra.

items.title: Voiding a question
items.text: If a question is thrown out and read again, use the void action in the More menu. Voiding takes back the points from answers on that question and corrects the affected quizzers' correct and incorrect counts, and it works out again whether anyone's quiz-out or strike-out has changed as a result. It leaves the fouls on that question alone. The replacement question keeps the same question number and the same value.

items.title: Match summary
items.text: Goal: close out the round and keep a record of it.

items.title: Getting to the summary
items.text: The Summary button in the bottom console comes to life once the match is complete. You can also open the summary from the strip that appears at the end of the round. Tapping Done on the summary returns you to the home screen.

items.title: What the summary shows
items.text:
• The final result — which team won, or that it was a tie — with both team totals.
  • A breakdown for each quizzer: their score, their numbers of correct and incorrect answers, and their fouls.
  • Each team's time-outs taken and challenges recorded.
  • A question-by-question review, with tags for interrupted and contested questions.
  • The end-of-round announcements the rulesets call for.

items.title: Saving a copy
items.text:
Two buttons save the round as a file:

  • PDF — a tidy, printable score sheet. It has the team totals, a table of each team's quizzers, and a question-by-question list, and it is laid out to be easy to read on paper.
  • Spreadsheet — a plain file with one row per quizzer and one row per question, for anyone keeping records in a spreadsheet program.

Either button opens your device's usual sharing window, so you choose where the file goes: email it, save it to a folder, send it to a printer, or share it with another app. Nothing is uploaded anywhere — the file only goes where you send it.

On a tablet the sharing window may offer fewer places to send the file than on a computer. If you are not sure where a saved file ended up, share it to an app you recognise, such as your email or a file storage app.

items.title: Keeping the round without saving a copy
items.text: You do not have to save anything. The round stays on the device under Resume round until you delete it, so you can open the summary again later.

items.title: Question navigator
items.text: Goal: read the round at a glance, and get back to any question.

items.title: What it is
items.text: The navigator is the row of question numbers on the live screen. Each number carries the marks for what happened on that question, so you can see the whole round without hunting. It is the digital version of the marks you would make on the paper scoresheet.

items.title: Reading the marks
items.text: Mark What it means On the paper sheet A value under the number (10, 20, 30) The question's value, once you have set it The point-value box A score beside a quizzer The question was answered — a + value for correct, a − half for incorrect The written score A circle around the number The question was interrupted The circled number A slash across the number The question was contested The contest slash An F by a quizzer's score That quizzer fouled The F mark A struck-through number The question was voided and read again The struck-out cell A plain number Not yet read An empty box The highlighted number The current question The question in progress

items.title: Moving to a question
items.text: Tap a number to look at that question. On the Classic screen the grid behaves the same way — tapping a cell moves you to that question. Remember that tapping a cell never scores it. Scoring always happens in the console. That catches people out at first, so it is worth saying twice.

items.title: Correcting an older question
items.text: Because you can move to any question, you can go back and correct one. Move to it, then score it as usual; the ruling is recorded against that question. See Undo & corrections.

items.title: Scrolling
items.text: A full match of twenty questions fits across the screen without scrolling on a tablet held sideways. If a match goes to overtime, the extra questions are added on the end, and the row scrolls to reach them.

items.title: Announcing the round
items.text: Reading from the navigator is a quick way to tell the room where things stand — which questions have been answered and how many are left. It shows the same information the paper sheet's marks do.

items.title: Score answers
items.text: Goal: record what happened on a question, correctly and with one tap.

items.title: The loop
items.text:
Every answer follows the same three steps, in this order:

  1. Set the value for the question — 10, 20, or 30.
  2. Tap the quizzer who answered.
  3. Tap CORRECT or INCORRECT.

The console expects that order. Until a question has a value and a quizzer selected, the CORRECT and INCORRECT buttons stay switched off.

items.title: Setting the value
items.text:
The app does not guess what each question is worth — it asks you. Tap the value row under the question numbers, or the SET VALUE button at the top of the screen, and choose 10, 20, or 30. The value row works the same way on both live screens.

Teen Bible Quiz questions are a mix of ten-point, twenty-point, and thirty-point questions; Junior Bible Quiz has its own mix. The ruleset decides how many of each there are.

You set the value before scoring. Once a question has been answered, its value locks, because changing it afterwards would change a score already given. If you set the wrong value, undo the answer first and set it again.

If a value breaks a rule of the ruleset — a thirty-point question at the start of a Junior Bible Quiz match, for example — the app shows a notice, but it never stops you. See Alerts.

items.title: Correct and incorrect
items.text:
Select a quizzer first, then tap:

  • CORRECT adds the question's full value to the team total and to that quizzer's own score. The app then moves on to the next question.
  • INCORRECT takes away half the question's value — a thirty-point question answered wrong is −15. This is the rulebook's rule, and it is the same in both built-in rulesets; see Rulesets. The app also moves on to the next question, unless the question was interrupted, in which case it is read again to the other team and you stay on it.

Three incorrect answers strike a quizzer out.

items.title: Choosing the quizzer
items.text: Tap a quizzer's card (Modern) or the label beside their row (Classic) to select them. The selected quizzer is highlighted, and the CORRECT, INCORRECT, and FOUL buttons come alive. Tap the quizzer again to deselect. Tapping a quizzer who is not at the table does nothing.

items.title: When the app will not let you score
items.text: Some answers do not make sense on a given question — a second correct answer on the same question, for instance, or two answers from the same team. When that happens, the CORRECT and INCORRECT buttons switch off and a line under the console explains why. A foul is always allowed, because a foul is not an answer.

items.title: When a quizzer quizzes out or strikes out
items.text: You do nothing extra. When a quizzer reaches the ruleset's number of correct answers — five in Teen Bible Quiz, six in Junior Bible Quiz — the app adds the quiz-out bonus for you and shows a notice. The same is true of a third incorrect answer and a third foul. See Alerts.

items.title: Fixing a mistake
items.text: If you tapped the wrong quizzer or the wrong button, tap UNDO and enter the right one. Undo takes back only the most recent ruling. See Undo & corrections.

items.title: Saving
items.text: There is nothing to save. Each tap is written to the tablet the moment you make it. See Autosave & recovery.

items.title: Set up a match
items.text: Goal: get from the home screen to the live scoring screen with the right rules and the right people in the right seats.

items.title: Start a new round
items.text: On the home screen, tap START A NEW ROUND. The Resume round list just below it is for rounds you have already begun and not finished — tapping one of those rows takes you straight back into that round. This page is about starting a fresh one.

items.title: Pick the rules
items.text:
Two tabs sit at the top of the setup screen: Teen Bible Quiz and Junior Bible Quiz. Tap the one you are playing.

A card under the tabs then describes the rules of that choice — how many questions there are and what they are worth, and the numbers for quizzing out, striking out, and fouling out. It also lists the limits for time-outs and contests. A quick read is a good way to confirm you have the right one.

The rules come from the season's ruleset, not from the match. If your league uses different numbers, that is a new ruleset rather than a setting here — see Rulesets.

items.title: Name the teams
items.text: By default each team carries the name of its side of the quiz box: Red and Green. You can keep those names or type your own — many scorekeepers enter the actual team or church names, which makes the summary easier to read later. If you clear a box by accident, the app puts the default back.

items.title: Set out the quizzers
items.text:
Each team has two numbers to set:

  • Seated — how many quizzers sit at the table. Teen Bible Quiz allows up to three seated quizzers and Junior Bible Quiz up to four; every team needs at least one.
  • Bench — how many extra quizzers are waiting to rotate in.

Use the + and − buttons to change each count. A name box appears for every quizzer, seated or on the bench. Each one is filled in with a sensible default such as Red 1 or Green 2; type over any of them, or leave them if you do not yet have the real names.

The order of the names matters. The first seated quizzer is Red 1, the second is Red 2, and so on. The scoreboard and the summary follow that order, so enter the names in the order the quizzers are actually sitting.

items.title: Choose how the scores look
items.text: Two cards, Modern and Classic, choose the layout of the live screen. Both keep score the same way. Your device remembers the last one you picked, but you can choose a different one just for this round here. See Modern vs Classic and Settings.

items.title: Start the round
items.text: Tap START ROUND. The live scoring screen opens. Everything you set on this screen is saved as the round begins, and from here on every tap is saved too.

items.title: Common mistakes
items.text:
• The same name twice. Two quizzers may share a name, but it makes the summary hard to read — give them something to tell them apart.
  • Too few or too many seated quizzers. This changes the scoreboard, so set it before you start if you can. You can still swap quizzers in during the round.
  • The wrong ruleset. The ruleset sets the point values and the limits, so a wrong one will score the match differently. Check the details card before you tap START ROUND.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
Goal: adjust the app for the device and the room it is used in.

There is no separate settings screen. The few settings that exist are small switches in the top corner of the home screen, plus the live view that the app remembers from your last round. Everything is saved on the device itself.

items.title: The switches in the top corner
items.text:
Three small buttons sit in the top corner of the home screen:

  • A light/dark switch. Tapping it moves between a light view, a dark view, and following whatever the tablet is set to. By default the app follows the tablet. The red and green team colors stay clear and easy to tell apart in both light and dark.
  • A vibration switch. This turns the small tap vibration on or off. It is off by default, so a fresh tablet cannot buzz or distract anyone during a match. Turn it on if you would like the confirmation when you score.
  • An About button. This shows the version of the app you are running, along with the license information.

items.title: The live view the app remembers
items.text: When you start a round and choose Modern or Classic on the setup screen, the app remembers that choice for next time. It is remembered per device, because the same tablet is often passed between scorekeepers. You can still pick the other one for a single round without changing the remembered default — just choose it again on the setup screen. See Modern vs Classic.

items.title: Sound
items.text: There is no sound setting, because the app never plays any sound at all. That is deliberate: an official match should never be interrupted by a tablet's noises. The app makes no beeps, clicks, or music, and it does not rely on any.

items.title: Accessibility
items.text: The app is made to be used by touch and to work with a screen reader. The buttons are large, and nothing is hidden behind a long press or a swipe. Notices appear as ordinary text, so a screen reader can read them aloud. See Alerts.

items.title: Where settings are kept
items.text: Settings are stored on the device only. They are not part of a round, and they are not shared between devices. Reinstalling the app resets them to their defaults.

items.title: The settings at a glance
items.text: Setting Choices Default Applies to Light or dark Light · Dark · Follow the tablet Follow the tablet This device Tap vibration On · Off Off This device Live view Modern · Classic Modern This device, remembered from your last round

items.title: Undo & corrections
items.text: Goal: fix a mis-tap without disturbing anything else that has already happened.

items.title: Where Undo is
items.text: Undo is a large button in the bottom console, on both live screens. It is always on screen, never hidden behind a long press, and its label tells you what it is about to take back — for example, UNDO — Red 2 correct.

items.title: What Undo does
items.text:
Undo rewinds the most recent ruling. Two things happen together:

  • The ruling is taken back, and the scores, the quizzer's counts, and any notices are worked out again from what is left.
  • The screen moves back to the question that ruling belonged to, so you are looking at the thing you are changing.

Undo is exact, not approximate. If you undo a correct answer that had quizzed a quizzer out, the quiz-out bonus goes away along with it, because the bonus only ever came from that answer. See Event-sourced scoring for why.

items.title: Going further back
items.text: Undo is not limited to the last tap. Press it again to step back one ruling at a time, right to the start of the round. Every ruling is kept in the round's saved history, so there is nothing you can spoil by going back.

items.title: Correcting an older question
items.text: On the Classic screen you can move to a question other than the current one — tap its cell in the grid to go there, then score as usual. The ruling remembers which question it belongs to, so a correction lands on the right one. The question numbers and the value row help you confirm you are in the right place first.

items.title: When not to use Undo
items.text: Undo takes back a ruling. It is not the way to throw out a question or to handle a contest — those have their own actions and buttons. If a question is voided and read again, that is a void, not an undo. See Fouls, contests, interruptions & time-outs.

items.title: Which download do I need?
items.text:
Every release includes a file for each kind of device. Find your device in the table below, download the matching file, then follow its guide.

Your device Download Guide Amazon Fire tablet (recommended) app-release.apk Amazon Fire HD 10 Any Android tablet or phone app-release.apk Other Android devices Windows PC or touchscreen laptop concordance-windows-x64.zip Windows Linux desktop concordance-linux-x64.tar.gz Linux Mac concordance-macos.zip macOS

items.title: Where to download
items.text: All of these files are on the project's Releases page. Take the newest release unless you have a reason to use an older one.

items.title: The recommended device
items.text: An Amazon Fire HD 10 tablet is what the app is built and tested around. It is held on its side, the way a book lies open, and it runs Concordance without any need for Google Play. Concordance was designed for tablets like this one, so it is the safest choice if you are buying a device for the job.

items.title: Before you start
items.text: There is nothing to sign up for. You do not need an account, and once the app is installed it works without any internet connection. Installing takes about a minute.

items.title: What to expect along the way
items.text:
• Every release includes a small text file called SHA256SUMS, which lists a short code for each download. It lets you check that the file you received is exactly the file the project built. See Verifying your download.
  • The Windows, Linux, and Mac versions are not yet signed, so your computer will show a warning the first time you open them. That warning is expected, and each guide explains exactly which button to press.

items.title: Related
items.text: • Updating & uninstalling

items.title: Other Android devices
items.text: Any Android tablet or phone can run Concordance from the same file the Fire tablet uses. If your device is an Amazon Fire tablet, use the Fire HD 10 page instead — the steps are a little different.

items.title: 1. Download the app
items.text: On the device, open your web browser and go to the project's Releases page. Tap the file called app-release.apk to download it.

items.title: 2. Allow this source to install apps
items.text:
Android will not install an app until you say the source is trusted. You do not have to hunt for the setting: when you open the downloaded file, Android will offer to install it and, if it is not already allowed, will send you to Settings. Switch on Allow from this source, then go back and tap Install.

If you would rather set it up ahead of time, open Settings, then Apps → Special access → Install unknown apps, and allow your browser or file manager there.

items.title: 3. The Play Protect warning
items.text: You may see a warning such as "Unsafe app blocked". Tap Install anyway (or More details, then Install anyway). This warning appears for any app that was not downloaded from the Play Store. It is not a sign that anything is wrong.

items.title: 4. Which devices work
items.text: Concordance is made for a tablet held sideways, the way a book lies open. A phone will run it for practice, but the buttons and the scoreboard are laid out for a screen the size of a tablet, so they will feel cramped on a phone. The app needs Android 7 or newer.

items.title: Related
items.text:
• Amazon Fire HD 10
  • Verifying your download

items.title: Amazon Fire HD 10 (recommended)
items.text: The Amazon Fire HD 10 is the tablet Concordance is built for. Fire tablets do not use Google Play, so there is nothing to install first — you download one file and open it. This page walks you through it.

items.title: 1. Download the app
items.text: On the tablet, open the web browser and go to the project's Releases page. Tap the file called app-release.apk to download it. Fire tablets come with a browser called Silk; if you prefer, you can copy the file onto the tablet from a computer and put it in the Downloads folder instead.

items.title: 2. Tell the tablet that this install is allowed
items.text:
Android will not install an app until you say the source is trusted. On a Fire tablet:

  1. Open Settings.
  2. Go to Security & Privacy.
  3. Turn on Apps from Unknown Sources. On newer Fire tablets this setting is called Install unknown apps, and you switch it on for the app you are installing from — usually Files or Silk.

items.title: 3. Install it
items.text: Open the Files app, open Downloads, and tap app-release.apk. If the tablet shows a warning that this type of file could be harmful, tap Install anyway. That warning appears for every app that did not come from an app store; it is normal, not a sign that anything is wrong.

items.title: 4. Open it, and find it again
items.text: When the install finishes, open the app. Its name is Concordance. New apps on a Fire tablet do not always land on the home screen — if you cannot see it, swipe up from the bottom of the home screen to open the App Library, and you will find it there.

items.title: 5. Get the tablet ready for a match
items.text:
Two quick changes make the tablet easier to keep score on:

  • Keep the screen awake. In Settings → Display, set the screen timeout to a long time, so the tablet does not go to sleep between questions.
  • Turn the tablet sideways. Concordance is designed for use in landscape (wide) view. In Settings → Display, turn off Auto-rotate screen so the picture does not tip when you set the tablet down.

items.title: 6. If the app will not install
items.text:
• "App not installed" — usually means a different copy of Concordance is already on the tablet, or the download did not finish. Remove any older copy of the app, then download the file again and retry.
  • Not enough space — check Settings → Storage and free up some room, then try again.
  • You cannot find the setting in step 2 — the wording differs a little between Fire tablets. Look under Security & Privacy for Apps from Unknown Sources, or for Install unknown apps.

items.text:
• Other Android devices
  • Install & launch problems

items.title: Linux
items.text: Concordance for Linux is a folder of files inside a single download. It does not come with an installer package yet. These steps use a terminal, which is a few short commands.

items.title: 1. Download it
items.text: Download concordance-linux-x64.tar.gz from the project's Releases page.

items.title: 2. Extract it
items.text:
Open a terminal in the folder where you downloaded the file and run:

tar -xzf concordance-linux-x64.tar.gz

That creates a folder called bundle.

items.title: 3. Run it
items.text:
./bundle/concordance

The file keeps its permission to run from the archive, so there is nothing extra to set up.

items.title: 4. If it says a library is missing
items.text:
If the app refuses to start with a message mentioning libgtk-3.so.0, your system is missing the GTK 3 library that the app draws its window with. Install it with your distribution's package manager:

# Debian / Ubuntu
sudo apt install libgtk-3-0

# Fedora
sudo dnf install gtk3

# Arch
sudo pacman -S gtk3

items.title: 5. If the window is blank or ignores clicks
items.text:
Concordance is tested on the classic Linux display system (called X11). If the window comes up blank, or your taps and clicks do nothing, start it like this instead:

GDK_BACKEND=x11 ./bundle/concordance

items.title: 6. Add it to your app menu (optional)
items.text:
To launch Concordance without a terminal, create a file named ~/.local/share/applications/concordance.desktop with these contents, changing the path to wherever you extracted bundle:

[Desktop Entry]
Name=Concordance
Exec=/home/you/Downloads/bundle/concordance
Type=Application
Categories=Utility;

items.title: 7. What is not available yet
items.text: There is no .deb, .rpm, or one-file AppImage download yet. The archive above is the only Linux download for now.

items.title: macOS
items.text: The Mac version is a normal app you drag into your Applications folder. The only tricky part is the first launch, which macOS blocks until you tell it the app is safe. This page covers both.

items.title: Which Mac you need
items.text: The download is built for Apple silicon Macs — the ones with an M1 chip or newer. On an older Intel Mac the app will not open, because the download contains only the Apple silicon version. Support for Intel Macs is something a future release may add.

items.title: 1. Download and unzip it
items.text: Download concordance-macos.zip from the project's Releases page, then double-click the zip file to unzip it. You get an app called Concordance.app.

items.title: 2. Move it into Applications
items.text: Drag Concordance.app into your Applications folder. If you leave it in your Downloads folder, macOS will make you step past a warning every single time you open it.

items.title: 3. Open it for the first time
items.text:
macOS will refuse the first launch, with a message such as "Concordance.app cannot be opened because the developer cannot be verified." This is macOS being careful about an app it does not recognise. There are two ways past it:

  • Right-click (or Control-click) the app, choose Open, then click Open again in the box that appears.
  • Or open the Terminal app and run this line:
xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Concordance.app

It tells macOS to stop treating the app as an unknown download. You only need to do this once.

items.title: 4. Why the warning appears
items.text: The Mac version is not signed or notarized by Apple. Notarizing an app requires a paid Apple developer account, which the project does not have yet. Until then, the steps above are the way in — and after that first launch, the app behaves like any other.

items.title: 5. Uninstalling
items.text: Drag Concordance.app from Applications to the Trash. Your saved rounds are not kept inside the app, so remove those too if you want them gone. See Data & storage and Updating & uninstalling.

items.title: Updating & uninstalling
items.text: Your saved rounds are kept outside the app itself, so an update keeps them and uninstalling deletes them. For where they are kept, see Data & storage.

items.title: Android and Fire tablets
items.text:
To update: download the newer app-release.apk and install it over the app that is already there. Your rounds are kept.

If you see "App not installed" during an update, it usually means the copy already on the device came from a different build. Uninstall the old app first, then install the new one — but note that uninstalling also deletes your rounds, so save anything you need first.

To uninstall: press and hold the app icon and choose Uninstall, or go to Settings → Apps, find Concordance, and uninstall it there.

items.title: Windows
items.text:
To update: download the new zip, extract it, and let it replace the old folder. Your rounds are stored elsewhere, so they are not affected.

To uninstall: delete the folder.

items.title: Linux
items.text:
To update: extract the new archive and replace the old bundle folder with the new one.

To uninstall: delete the bundle folder.

items.title: macOS
items.text:
To update: download the new zip, unzip it, and drag the new Concordance.app into Applications, replacing the old one. Because macOS marks every download as unknown, you will need to repeat the right-click Open step from the macOS page after updating.

To uninstall: drag the app to the Trash, then remove its data folder if you also want your rounds gone — see Data & storage.

items.title: Before you uninstall
items.text: Uninstalling removes your saved rounds along with the app. If a match matters to you, save it first as a PDF or a spreadsheet file — see Match summary.

items.title: Verifying your download
items.text: Every release includes a small text file called SHA256SUMS. It lists a long code for each file in the release. Checking those codes confirms that the file you downloaded is exactly the file the project built — worth doing for something you install on a tablet.

items.title: What the file looks like
items.text:
Open SHA256SUMS in any text editor. Each line has a long code, a couple of spaces, and a file name:

<long code>  app-release.apk
<long code>  concordance-windows-x64.zip
<long code>  concordance-linux-x64.tar.gz
<long code>  concordance-macos.zip

items.title: Linux
items.text:
Put SHA256SUMS in the same folder as your download, open a terminal there, and run:

sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS

The word OK appears next to each file that matches.

items.title: macOS
items.text:
In Terminal, run:

shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS

items.title: Windows
items.text:
Windows does not read the file for you. In the folder with your download, open a Command Prompt and run this, using the name of the file you downloaded:

certutil -hashfile concordance-windows-x64.zip SHA256

It prints a code. Compare it, character for character, with the matching line in SHA256SUMS. Every character has to be the same — there is no such thing as a close match.

items.title: Android and Fire tablets
items.text: Tablets cannot check these codes on their own. If you want to be sure, check the file on a computer first, then copy it across to the tablet.

items.title: If the codes do not match
items.text: Do not install the file; the download could have been tampered with and may be harmful to your device. Delete it, download it again, and check once more. If it still does not match, please report it — a mismatch should never be ignored. See the security policy for how to get in touch.

items.title: Windows
items.text: Concordance comes to Windows as a folder of files rather than a setup program. This page shows you how to get it running the first time.

items.title: 1. Download it
items.text: On your PC, open the project's Releases page and download the file called concordance-windows-x64.zip.

items.title: 2. Unzip it
items.text:
Right-click the downloaded file and choose Extract All…, then extract it somewhere you will remember — your Desktop or your Documents folder is fine.

This step matters. The app has to run from the unzipped folder, because it needs the other files that came with it. Opening concordance.exe from inside the zip will not work.

items.title: 3. Run it
items.text: Open the unzipped folder and double-click concordance.exe. The very first time you open it, Windows takes a few seconds to get it ready; later launches are faster. That delay is normal.

items.title: 4. The first-launch warning
items.text:
You will probably see a blue box titled "Windows protected your PC". Windows shows this for any app it does not recognise, and Concordance is not yet signed, so the warning is expected:

  1. Click More info.
  2. Click Run anyway.

The app opens normally after that, and you will not be asked again on this PC.

items.title: 5. Make it easy to find
items.text: Right-click concordance.exe and choose Pin to Start. Then the scorekeeper can launch it from the Start menu instead of digging through Downloads.

items.title: 6. Touch and display
items.text: Concordance opens in a wide window, ready for a touchscreen laptop. You do not need a keyboard to keep score — every button is large enough to tap. There is no installer yet; the app is a folder you keep and run, and a signed installer is planned for a later release.

items.title: Data & storage
items.text: Goal: answer "where is my data, and who can see it?"

items.title: What is kept
items.text:
Two things:

  • Your rounds. Each round, with every ruling you recorded in it, is kept so it can be opened again later. The scores are worked out from those rulings rather than stored on their own.
  • Your settings. The light/dark choice, the tap-vibration choice, and the last live view you used.

Nothing else is stored. There are no accounts, no usage tracking, and no information about you.

items.title: Where it is kept
items.text:
Rounds are kept in a single file called concordance.db, in the app's own folder on your device. The exact folder depends on the platform:

Platform Where the file is Android / Fire The app's private storage, not visible in a normal file manager Windows %APPDATA%\Concordance\Concordance\concordance.db Linux ~/.local/share/org.concordance.concordance/concordance.db macOS ~/Library/Application Support/org.concordance.app/concordance.db

Your settings are kept separately, in the place your device normally keeps an app's small preferences.

items.title: How it is written
items.text:
Your rulings are written to the file as you make them. Each change is written in one piece, so if the tablet loses power in the middle of a write, the round is left at the state it was in before that change — never half-applied.

When you reopen a round, the scores are worked out again from the rulings on record. That is what makes undo exact, as described in Autosave & recovery.

items.title: What is not kept
items.text:
• No account, and no sign-in of any kind.
  • No names of real people, beyond the team and quizzer names you type in yourself.
  • No usage tracking, no analytics, and no crash reports.
  • No network activity at all — the app never connects to the internet.

items.title: Keeping a copy
items.text: Saving a round as a PDF or a spreadsheet file is the supported way to keep a copy, and it is the only way we recommend. On a desktop computer you can also copy the concordance.db file itself, but that is not supported and a copy cannot be loaded back in — it is there for emergencies only.

items.title: Deleting data
items.text:
There are three levels, each with a different effect:

What you do What is removed Delete one round from the home screen That round only. You are asked to confirm first. Uninstall the app All rounds and your settings Clear the app's storage (Android/Fire) All rounds and your settings

Uninstalling removes your rounds for good, so save anything you care about first. See Updating & uninstalling.

items.title: Glossary
items.text: Goal: define the terms the sport and the app use, all in one place.

items.title: Quiz terms
items.text: Term What it means Quiz box The table where the quizzers sit and buzz in. The two sides of it are the Red team and the Green team. Quizzer A contestant on one of the two teams. Seat A quizzer's position at the table. The seats are numbered in order (Red 1, Red 2, Green 1, and so on). Bench A team's quizzers who are not sitting at the table. They can be swapped in during the match. Substitute A bench quizzer who swaps in for a seated quizzer. Question value How many points a question is worth: 10, 20, or 30. Correct answer An answer accepted by the officials. It earns the question's full value. Incorrect answer A rejected answer. It takes off half the question's value. Half-value deduction The rule that an incorrect answer costs half of what the question was worth — a 30-point question answered wrong is −15. Interruption A quizzer buzzing in before the question has finished being read. Contest A team's formal challenge to a ruling, in Teen Bible Quiz. Coach's Appeal The same idea in Junior Bible Quiz; two are allowed per team. Void A question thrown out and read again, keeping the same question number and value. Quiz out A quizzer reaching the ruleset's number of correct answers, which also earns a bonus. Strike out A quizzer reaching the ruleset's number of incorrect answers. Foul out A quizzer reaching the ruleset's number of fouls. Personal foul A foul charged to one quizzer. Team foul A foul charged to the whole team, such as a coach's foul. Time-out A short pause requested by a team. Each team has a limited number. Overtime question An extra question added when a match is tied after the last regulation question. Match and round One game between the two teams, from the first question to the last. Question number A question's place in the round, from 1 to 20 in regulation.

items.title: App terms
items.text: Term What it means Round One match's worth of scoring in the app. A round is what you start, resume, or delete. Ruling Anything you record — an answer, a foul, an interruption, a time-out. Console The strip of large buttons along the bottom of the live screen. All scoring happens here. Navigator The row of question numbers on the live screen. See Question navigator. Mark A symbol on the navigator showing what happened on a question, such as a circle for an interruption. Modern view The live screen laid out as two team halves. Classic view The live screen laid out as a scoresheet grid. Notice (or alert) A message the app shows above the console, such as a quiz-out. See Alerts. Undo The button that takes back the most recent ruling. See Undo & corrections. Autosave The app's habit of saving every ruling the moment you make it. Resume Opening a saved round and carrying on where you left off. Ruleset The set of numbers that describes one rulebook, such as Teen Bible Quiz 2025-26. See Rulesets. Export Saving a finished round as a PDF (a printable score sheet) or a spreadsheet file. See Match summary.

items.title: Release artifacts & checksums
items.text: Goal: know exactly what each release contains and how it is produced.

items.title: What a release contains
items.text: File Platform Notes app-release.apk Android / Fire (recommended) The app file for tablets and phones concordance-windows-x64.zip Windows A folder of files to run concordance-linux-x64.tar.gz Linux A folder of files to run concordance-macos.zip macOS The app, ready to drag into Applications SHA256SUMS — One code per file above, for checking a download

items.title: How a release is made
items.text: When the project publishes a new version, a single build makes all four files from the same set of code and attaches them to the release, together with the SHA256SUMS file. Because every file in a release comes from one build, a download can always be tied back to the exact version it came from.

items.title: Where to get it
items.text: The Releases page is the place to download. You may occasionally see temporary builds attached to the project's other pages while a version is being prepared; those are only for testing and should be ignored. The Releases page always holds the builds meant for use.

items.title: Are the files signed?
items.text:
• The Android and Fire app file is signed, using the project's own signing key. That signature is what lets a new version install over an older one.
  • The Windows, Linux, and Mac builds are not signed yet, and the Mac app is also not notarized. That is why your computer shows a warning the first time you open them — each install page explains which button to press. Signed desktop builds are planned for a later release.

items.title: Checking a download
items.text: Every release includes the SHA256SUMS file so you can confirm a download is genuine. The steps are on Verifying your download.

items.title: Rulesets
items.text: Goal: understand how Concordance knows the rules, and which numbers are built in.

items.title: Rules as data, not code
items.text:
Everything that changes from one rulebook to another lives in a ruleset file rather than in the app's code. That means how many questions there are, what they are worth, how a correct answer is scored, how many wrong answers strike a quizzer out, and the limits on time-outs and challenges.

Because of this, a new season is a new ruleset file, and the app does not need updating to score it. Rulesets are never removed, so a round from a past season can still be scored exactly the way it was played.

items.title: The two built-in rulesets
items.text:
• Teen Bible Quiz for the 2025-26 season → TBQ preset
  • Junior Bible Quiz for 2026 → JBQ preset

items.title: Choosing a ruleset
items.text: You choose the ruleset when you set up a round, on the tabs at the top of the setup screen. The choice applies to that round.

items.title: Where the numbers come from
items.text: The numbers in a ruleset come from the official rulebooks. This wiki records only the numbers needed to keep score — it does not restate the rules themselves. The official rulebooks are the authority, and where this wiki and a rulebook disagree, the rulebook wins.

items.title: A note on the rulebooks
items.text: The rulebooks are copyrighted and licensed for local church use only. They are not copied into or published with this app or this wiki. What you will find here are the numbers the app needs, together with a pointer to the official book for the rules themselves.

items.title: Adding a ruleset
items.text: A new ruleset is a single file, and no changes to the app are needed to support it. The format is described on the Ruleset schema page, and the contributing guide explains how to add one.

items.title: JBQ preset (Junior Bible Quiz, 2026)
items.text:
Ruleset id: jbq-2026 → assets/rulesets/jbq-2026.json

Junior Bible Quiz is one of the two rulesets built into Concordance. This page lists the numbers it uses to keep score.

items.title: The match
items.text:
• Two teams.
  • Twenty questions: ten worth 10 points, seven worth 20, and three worth 30.
  • Seated quizzers: at least one and at most four per team, with up to eight quizzers on a team's roster in total.
  • The rulebook also fixes where the values may fall — no 30-point question at either end of the match, none back to back, and at least three 20s and one 30 in each half. The app shows a notice if a value breaks these, but it never stops you. See Alerts.

items.title: Answers
items.text:
• Correct: the full value of the question.
  • Incorrect: half the value taken off — a 30-point question answered wrong is −15.

items.title: Quizzing out, striking out, fouling out
items.text:
• Quiz out: a quizzer's sixth correct answer. It adds a +10 bonus, and the quizzer leaves the match.
  • Strike out: a quizzer's third incorrect answer, and the quizzer leaves the match.
  • Foul: −5, shown as an F on the quizzer. A quizzer's third foul is a foul out. A foul by someone other than a quizzer — a coach, for example — is charged to the team.

items.title: Time-outs and Coach's Appeals
items.text:
• Time-outs: three per team in regulation, with the app notifying on a fourth request.
  • Coach's Appeals: two per team. Each is recorded as successful or unsuccessful, and further appeals are refused once a team's allowance is used.

items.title: Overtime
items.text: If the match is level after twenty questions, overtime begins with one 10-point, one 20-point, and one 30-point question, then continues with 20-point questions until the tie is broken. Any time-outs a team has left carry into overtime, plus one extra.

items.title: What is the same as TBQ
items.text:
Junior Bible Quiz and Teen Bible Quiz share a good deal: two teams, twenty questions, the shape of correct and incorrect scoring, the number of wrong answers that strike a quizzer out, and the way fouls work. Of note, a quizzer who quizzes out or strikes out leaves the match in Junior Bible Quiz, whereas in Teen Bible Quiz a quizzer who quizzes out stays in.

The full list of differences is in the table on the TBQ preset page.

Rulebooks govern

These are the numbers the preset uses. The official JBQ rulebook is the authority, and nothing on this page restates it.

items.title: TBQ preset (Teen Bible Quiz, 25-26)
items.text:
Ruleset id: tbq-25-26 → assets/rulesets/tbq-25-26.json

Teen Bible Quiz is one of the two rulesets built into Concordance. This page lists the numbers it uses to keep score.

items.title: The match
items.text:
• Two teams.
  • Twenty questions: eight worth 10 points, nine worth 20, and three worth 30.
  • Seated quizzers: at least one and at most three per team. There is no limit on how many extra quizzers a team may keep on the bench.

items.title: Answers
items.text:
• Correct: the full value of the question.
  • Incorrect: half the value taken off — a 30-point question answered wrong is −15.

items.title: Quizzing out, striking out, fouling out
items.text:
• Quiz out: a quizzer's fifth correct answer. It adds a +20 bonus. The quizzer stays in the match.
  • Strike out: a quizzer's third incorrect answer.
  • Foul: −5. A quizzer's third foul is a foul out. A foul charged to the team itself (a coach's foul, for example) takes 5 off the team total.

items.title: Time-outs and contests
items.text:
• Time-outs: three per team in regulation. A fourth request is not counted, and a team foul is owed — the app tells you, and you record the foul.
  • Contests: recorded as successful or unsuccessful. The app notifies the scorekeeper on a team's third unsuccessful contest, and refuses any further contests from that team. Up to two contests per question per team.

items.title: Overtime
items.text: If the match is level after twenty questions, overtime begins with 10-point questions, taken one at a time until the tie is broken. No time-outs may be taken in overtime.

items.title: How TBQ differs from JBQ
items.text:
Teen Bible Quiz Junior Bible Quiz Questions 20 20 Value mix eight 10s, nine 20s, three 30s ten 10s, seven 20s, three 30s Quiz out 5th correct, +20 bonus 6th correct, +10 bonus On quizzing out Stays in the match Leaves the match Strike out 3rd incorrect 3rd incorrect Challenge Contest Coach's Appeal Challenge limit 3rd unsuccessful notifies 2 per team Seated quizzers up to 3 up to 4 Overtime time-outs none leftover time-outs plus one

Rulebooks govern

These are the numbers the preset uses. The official TBQ rulebook is the authority, and nothing on this page restates it.

items.title: Troubleshooting & FAQ
items.text:
Something is wrong? Start here.

A round that is already in progress is saved as you go, so the first thing to try with almost any problem is to close the app completely and open it again.

items.title: Find your problem
items.text: What you are seeing Where to look An app file will not install on a tablet Install & launch problems Windows says it protected your PC Install & launch problems macOS will not open the app Install & launch problems The app closes straight away Install & launch problems The screen goes blank on Linux Install & launch problems A round seems to have disappeared Recovering a round A question or a whole round looks wrong Recovering a round A general question FAQ

items.title: The first thing to try
items.text: Most problems go away when you close the app completely and open it again. Your round is saved as you go, so nothing is lost by doing this, and the round comes back where you left it.

items.title: Asking for help
items.text:
If you need to report a problem, these details make it far easier to help:

  • the device you are using and its version (for example, "Amazon Fire HD 10"),
  • the version of the app, which you can see by tapping About on the home screen,
  • what you tapped just before the problem happened,
  • a screenshot, if you can take one.

You can report a bug or ask a question on the project's issues page.

items.title: Related
items.text:

  • Recovering a round
  • FAQ

items.title: Recovering a round
items.text: First: do not panic, and do not uninstall the app. Everything you had already recorded was written to the device. Opening the app again is safe, and uninstalling would remove the very thing you are trying to save.

items.title: The round is not on the home screen
items.text: Look through the Resume round list carefully. Each saved round is labelled with its two team names, so look for the names you used. If you see a different set of names, you may be looking at the list just after starting a new round — the earlier one should still be there too.

items.title: The app closed, or the tablet ran out of battery
items.text: Open the app and resume the round from the home screen. The scores are worked out again from everything you recorded, including your undo history, so you land on the same screen with the same numbers. See Autosave & recovery.

items.title: The app will not open at all
items.text:
• Android / Fire: install the app again over the top of the old one. As long as it is the same app from the same source, your rounds are kept. Installing an app that was signed by a different key forces Android to remove the old one first, and that deletes your rounds — so only install the official download.
  • Windows and Linux: your rounds are not stored inside the app's folder, so replacing or re-extracting that folder does not touch them.
  • macOS: replacing the app in Applications does not touch your rounds either.

items.title: The last tap is missing
items.text: If the very last thing you recorded is gone, the app closed in the moment between your tap and the change being written down. Re-enter that one ruling and carry on. You will never see a ruling half-applied, because each change is saved in one piece.

items.title: Continuing without the old round
items.text: There is no way to bring a round in from a file. If you need to carry on from a score you can see but cannot reopen, start a new round, set the scores up as they were, and continue from there. Be aware that the old round's history stays with the old round.

items.title: If the round really matters
items.text: If a round is important and it will not open, stop before you do anything else. Do not uninstall the app, and do not delete any rounds. Then open an issue on the project's issues page and describe what happened. Include the app version (from the About button), your device, and what you saw.

items.title: Is Concordance an official Bible Quiz app?
items.text: No. It is an independent community project, not affiliated with or endorsed by Bible Quiz, and it is not the scorekeeper of record for official matches. Personal, practice, and unofficial use is welcome.

items.title: Does it need the internet?
items.text: No, not at any point. It never connects to anything. See Offline-only, no accounts.

items.title: Will it work on my device?
items.text: It runs on Amazon Fire tablets, other Android tablets and phones, Windows, Linux, and Mac. Find your device in the table on Which download do I need?.

items.title: Is it free? What is its license?
items.text: Yes, it is free. It is open source under the AGPL-3.0-only license.

items.title: Does it work on an iPad?
items.text: Not yet. The toolkit the app is built with does not currently support iPads, so it is not something an upcoming release is likely to add soon.

items.title: Can I run a whole tournament with it?
items.text: Not yet. One round at a time is what the app does today; running a schedule or several matches at once is not part of it.

items.title: Does it show the questions?
items.text: No. It records what happens on each question — correct, incorrect, interrupted, contested — but it does not display question text or tracks.

items.title: Can I fix a mistake?
items.text: Yes. Tap Undo, which takes back the most recent ruling. See Undo & corrections.

items.title: Will it lose my round if the battery dies?
items.text: No. Everything is saved as you go. See Autosave & recovery.

items.title: Can I use it alongside the paper scoresheet?
items.text: Yes. It records the same marks the paper sheet does, so it works well as a backup or a second copy. See Question navigator.

items.title: Why is there no big scoreboard for the room?
items.text: Concordance is a scorekeeper's tool, not a display. It shows the score to the person keeping it, and it does not add a projector or audience view.

items.title: Does it make any sound?
items.text: No, never. That is deliberate: a match should not be disturbed by a tablet's noises. See Settings.

items.title: Which rulebook versions are built in?
items.text: Teen Bible Quiz (2025-26) and Junior Bible Quiz (2026). See Rulesets.

items.title: My league uses different numbers. Can I change them?
items.text: Yes, by adding a ruleset file; no changes to the app are needed. See Ruleset schema.

items.title: Where do the rules come from, and why are they not quoted here?
items.text: They come from the official rulebooks, which are copyrighted and licensed for local church use only, so this wiki does not reproduce them. It lists only the numbers the app needs. See Rulesets.

items.title: I found a bug. What do you need from me?
items.text: Open an issue on the project's issues page. Include your device, the app version (from the About button), what you tapped, and a screenshot if you can.

items.title: Can I help?
items.text: Yes, contributions are welcome. See the contributing guide.

items.title: Install & launch problems
items.text: Every problem below is set out the same way: what you see, why it happens, and how to fix it.

items.title: "App not installed"
items.text:
Why: the most common cause is that a different copy of the app is already on the tablet; a new install cannot replace one that was signed by someone else. Less often, the download did not finish, or the tablet is out of storage.

Fix: remove any older copy of Concordance first, then install again. If that does not help, free up some storage and download the file once more.

items.title: "This type of file can harm your device"
items.text:
Why: this is the warning Android shows for any app that did not come from an app store. It is not a sign that anything is wrong with this particular file.

Fix: if you are confident you downloaded it from the project's Releases page, tap Install anyway.

items.title: The "unknown sources" setting is missing or greyed out
items.text:
Why: newer versions of Android and Fire OS move this permission to the app you are installing from, rather than having one switch for everything.

Fix: open Settings and look under Security & Privacy for Install unknown apps, then allow your browser or file manager there. On older devices, look for a single Apps from Unknown Sources switch instead.

items.title: The app installed but there is no icon for it
items.text:
Why: Fire tablets do not always put a new app on the home screen.

Fix: swipe up from the bottom of the home screen to open the App Library, and look for it there.

items.title: "Windows protected your PC"
items.text:
Why: Windows shows this for any app it does not recognise, and Concordance is not yet signed.

Fix: click More info, then Run anyway.

items.title: Nothing happens when you double-click the app
items.text:
Why: the app was opened from inside the zip file, rather than from the folder you extracted it to.

Fix: right-click the zip and choose Extract All… first, then run concordance.exe from the extracted folder.

items.title: A message about a missing file
items.text:
Why: the same cause as above — the app needs the other files that came in the zip, and it cannot find them from inside the zip.

Fix: run the app from the extracted folder, with all of its files beside it.

items.title: "error while loading shared libraries: libgtk-3.so.0"
items.text:
Why: the app needs the GTK 3 library to draw its window, and your system does not have it installed.

Fix: install GTK 3 with your package manager. The exact command for each common distribution is on the Linux page.

items.title: The window is blank, or clicks do nothing
items.text:
Why: Concordance is tested on the classic Linux display system (called X11), and some other setups do not agree with it.

Fix: start the app in that mode — the command is on the Linux page.

items.title: "Permission denied"
items.text:
Why: the app was run from inside the archive rather than extracted first.

Fix: extract the archive, then run the app from the extracted folder.

items.title: "cannot be opened because the developer cannot be verified"
items.text:
Why: the app is not signed or notarized by Apple, so macOS is careful about it.

Fix: right-click (or Control-click) the app, choose Open, then click Open again in the box. The other method is described on the macOS page.

items.title: "The app is damaged and can't be opened"
items.text:
Why: the tool that unzipped the download did not preserve the app's internal links.

Fix: use your Mac's own unzip — double-click the zip file in Finder — rather than a third-party tool.

items.title: The app will not open on an older Intel Mac
items.text:
Why: the download is built for Apple silicon Macs, so it will not run on an older Intel Mac.

Fix: there is no fix yet. You can open an issue on the project's issues page to ask about Intel support.

items.title: The app opens but the round looks empty
items.text:
Why: you may have started a new round rather than opening the one you were using.

Fix: return to the home screen and open your round from the Resume round list.
